title: Last Execution for Witchcraft in Poland: End of European Capital Prosecution
description: The last formal execution for witchcraft in Poland occurred in 1793, making Poland one of the last European countries to end capital punishment for witchcraft. Polish witch trials had continued later than in most of Western Europe, reflecting the persistence of legal frameworks and local religious culture in the eastern European periphery of the Catholic world. The Polish cases in the later eighteenth century share the pattern seen elsewhere of isolated local prosecutions continuing in peripheral areas long after central authorities had abandoned the practice. With the late Polish executions, the era of European capital punishment for witchcraft effectively ended, though popular witch belief, village-level accusation, and informal lynching continued.
historiographical_note: Brian Levack's European statistics on the total execution toll acknowledge the difficulty of the Polish data. The persistence of formal prosecution into the 1790s in Poland, while Western Europe had largely abandoned execution decades earlier, illustrates the geographic unevenness of Enlightenment influence on legal practice — a theme central to Levack's comparative approach.
source_method: Levack, The Witch-Hunt in Early Modern Europe (1987); secondary scholarship on Polish witch trials
scholarly_disagreement: The exact year and circumstances of the last Polish execution are debated in Polish historical literature; some sources give slightly different dates. The figure of 1793 is the most commonly cited in English-language scholarship.
